text:
The company will adopt a tiered retention schedule that distinguishes between raw personal data and anonymized audit records to satisfy both GDPR storage limitation principles and the security lead's requirement for one year of audit logs. For Application Logs, raw data containing user identifiers and free text will be retained for 30 days to support active customer support investigations. After this period, an automated pseudonymization process will replace user IDs with opaque tokens and redact identifiable free text fields, converting the logs into non-personal audit data retained for 12 months. Infrastructure Logs containing IP addresses will be hashed at ingestion; raw IPs are accessible only for 30 days to resolve active support tickets, after which the hashed hashes remain for 6 months for security forensics under a legitimate interest basis. Database backups will follow the current 90-day cycle for operational recovery, with cryptographic erasure enforced upon termination of individual customer accounts. Audit Logs, representing the final state of all system activities, will be retained for 12 months as required by law and security policy.

To honor the contractual promise of deleting a customer's data within 30 days of termination, the company employs a technical mechanism where 'deletion' is defined as the rendering of data non-personal rather than immediate physical destruction. For Application Logs, a scheduled job runs at Day 30 to tokenize all user IDs and apply context-aware redaction to free text fields, ensuring that any remaining content cannot be linked back to an individual without additional information held by the company. For Infrastructure Logs, IP addresses are immediately hashed upon ingestion; while raw IPs are available for the first 30 days, post-Day 30 logs contain only hashed values that do not constitute personal data under GDPR Recital 26, as re-identification is technically impossible without the original hashing keys which are destroyed. For Backups, the system uses logical deletion (soft deletes) combined with key rotation; upon customer termination, the encryption keys for that specific customer's backup blob are destroyed, rendering the data unreadable and effectively 'deleted' while preserving the structural snapshot for general disaster recovery.

The retention schedule is enforced by automated scripts managed by the engineering team, removing the need for a dedicated compliance function. For Application Logs, a daily ETL pipeline runs pseudonymization jobs targeting customers with an end-date less than 30 days in the future. For Infrastructure Logs, the log ingestion service applies one-way hashing immediately, ensuring no raw IPs are stored long-term. For Backups, the database engine enforces logical deletion flags and key rotation policies at the storage level. Proof of compliance is generated by a 'Compliance Audit Log' that records the success or failure of each automated job without storing any customer-identifiable information. This log includes timestamps, job IDs, and status codes, providing an immutable record of the process execution. The engineering team reviews these logs weekly to ensure automated jobs are running correctly, satisfying the GDPR accountability principle (Article 5(2)) by demonstrating that deletion processes were executed as designed.

The policy rests on specific GDPR concepts applied precisely to avoid overclaiming. For the initial 30-day retention of raw data, the legal basis is Contractual Necessity (Article 6(1)(b)), as retaining access to logs is required to provide support services and honor the service level agreement. After Day 30, the Application Logs become non-personal audit data; since they no longer constitute personal data under Recital 26, the GDPR storage limitation principle no longer applies, allowing retention for 12 months for legal defense and security auditing. For Infrastructure Logs hashed after 30 days, the 6-month retention of the raw IP data (while accessible) is justified by Legitimate Interest (Article 6(1)(f)) for security purposes, subject to a balancing test against user rights. The 30-day deletion promise is upheld because GDPR allows erasure when processing is no longer necessary or lawful; once data is pseudonymized or hashed such that re-identification is impossible, the 'personal data' obligation ends, satisfying the contract without violating the legal requirement to retain audit trails for one year.
